_comment: TEACHING LOG - what actually happened in each class, as opposed to what was planned.
Deliberately a SEPARATE file from schedule.json. schedule.json holds facts that are
synced from Moodle and can be regenerated; this holds hand-written judgement that must
never be clobbered by a regeneration. The master-schedule viewer merges the two by date.
Purpose: when the schedule is rebuilt for next year, this is the evidence for what to
move, cut, or give more room. Write the entry the same day if possible - the 'what I
wish I'd had time for' is the part that evaporates fastest.
Keys are ISO dates matching a class day in schedule.json.
Every field is optional; a two-line entry beats no entry.
covered   what actually got done, in a sentence or two
timing    actual minutes per segment. The nominal 50-minute plan is
kickoff 5, lecture 15, explore 20, synthesis 10
cut       what got dropped for time
wish      what you wish there had been time for
landed    what visibly worked - worth protecting next year
struggled what students got stuck on

nextYear  a direct instruction to whoever rebuilds this schedule
  notes     anything else worth remembering about the day
Example of the shape (not a real class):
"covered": "...", "timing": {"kickoff": 8, "lecture": 20, "explore": 14, "synthesis": 6},
"cut": "...", "wish": "...", "landed": "...", "struggled": "...", "nextYear": "..."
'materials' lists things made for the course this semester - worksheets, handouts,
skeleton notes. 'usedOn' is an ISO date once known; leave it null rather than guessing.
Per-day entries can also carry a 'materials' list naming what was handed out that day.

2026-10-28.covered: Went over the kickoff (KO22, a couple of Amperian-loop questions) -- went fine. Gave a brief lecture on Ampere's law, not stressed too heavily, drawing the comparison to Coulomb's law and Gauss's law; used it to re-derive B for a long straight wire (same result Biot-Savart gave earlier in the unit). Introduced the solenoid B-field and worked a sample problem -- Knight Section 29.6, Example 29.9 (how many loops a solenoid needs to produce the field required for an MRI machine). Then moved on into the Lorentz force F=qv x B, again drawing the electric-vs-magnetic parallel (same equation, just with a v-cross term), ran a set of clicker-style conceptual questions with moving charges (mentioned the Aurora Borealis, which got good student questions), and closed with a numerical example. This ran ahead into material the schedule had slated for Oct 30 (Lorentz force / magnetic force on moving charges).
2026-10-28.landed: The Aurora Borealis mention during the Lorentz-force clicker questions landed well -- got a couple of good follow-up questions, genuinely engaged the class.
2026-10-28.nextYear: Seth is reconsidering whether Ampere's law earns its own class day at all. The course doesn't lean on calculus much, and he's increasingly feeling students need more algebra practice instead -- floated not giving Ampere's law separate treatment next year and keeping the class moving (not a decision yet, just an open question to revisit when rebuilding the schedule).

2026-10-26.covered: Reverted to a slide deck (Magnetism.pptx, 30 slides) for the B-field intro lecture rather than lecture notes or the whiteboard -- Seth felt this worked well. Order: magnet basics (poles attract/repel, Earth as a magnet, the 'you can't cut a magnet into its two poles' tree diagram making the no-monopole point right at the start, 'all magnets are electromagnets'); B-field of a single moving charge (B = mu0/4pi * qv x rhat/r^2) with several right-hand-rule direction-practice questions for both + and - charges, including the r-parallel-to-v zero-field case; B-field of a straight wire via two RHR forms (thumb-curl-around-the-wire, and a compass-under-the-wire question), paired explicitly against the E-field-of-a-line-of-charge analogy (same 1/r falloff, same superposition logic: 'the whole wire influences the B-field, but the closer parts matter more'); building up Biot-Savart (dB = mu0/4pi * I dl x rhat/r^2) as the generalization from a single moving charge to a current element; B at the center of a current loop (B = mu0 I/2R) with an RHR direction-practice question for loop current; the full dipole-shaped field outside the loop's plane, explicitly compared to a bar magnet's N/S field pattern. Got through everything up to the solenoid material and stopped there -- did not reach stacking loops into a solenoid, the solenoid RHR, B = mu0 n I, or the closing 'charge flies into a solenoid' force problem (F=0 since v is parallel to B on-axis); those carry over to the next class.
2026-10-26.landed: The slide-deck approach for this lecture -- Seth felt it was pretty good for introducing the magnetic field. Specific things that landed: making the no-monopole point right at the start via the 'can't cut a magnet into two poles' diagram; the line-of-charge/line-of-current parallel (both fields drop like 1/r, both built by superposition, closer parts matter more); the dipole-shaped field outside the loop's plane being identical to an electric dipole's (and to a bar magnet's), while still being made of field lines that never terminate -- there's no magnetic monopole to cut them in half.
2026-10-26.struggled: KO21 (this morning's kickoff, before today's class) opened with a Biot-Savart plug-in question using the law's explicit magnitude form (dB = (mu0/4pi) I dl sin(theta)/r^2). That magnitude form wasn't actually built up until today's slides (the Biot-Savart generalization step, roughly slide 15) -- the 2026-10-23 class only reached B's direction, not magnitude. So KO21 tested a formula students hadn't seen in either class yet, and that took extra explaining at the start of today's class.
2026-10-26.nextYear: Seth feels this lecture (magnet basics -> no-monopole intro -> RHR practice with individual charges -> wire -> loop -> dipole-shape comparison, slide-deck based) should have come before the 2026-10-23 Biot-Savart-math lecture, not after -- reorder next year so the conceptual/RHR intuition-building happens first. Relatedly: whichever kickoff tests the Biot-Savart magnitude formula needs to run after a class has actually covered that magnitude form (today's slide ~15), not the morning before it -- KO21 this year landed one class session too early. Also: the solenoid material (stack-of-loops, solenoid RHR, B=mu0nI, charge-flies-into-a-solenoid problem) didn't get covered today and rolls into the next class -- budget time for it explicitly rather than assuming it fits after the loop material.

2026-10-23.covered: Kickoff (quick) on B-field direction from a moving charge/line of charge. Then spent a while going back over Test 3 to address misconceptions: Kirchhoff's loop rule and the junction rule (the junction equation as I1 + I2 + I3 = 0 is confusing since it's not obviously a conservation statement at a glance), and the RC discharge time constant. Then into today's Biot-Savart intro lecture notes (biot-savart-intro-notes.tex): worked through the separation vectors and unit separation vectors for the three E-field warm-up points (Section 1), then introduced the Biot-Savart law by framing it as Coulomb's law with an extra v-cross term inserted (Section 2) -- got through the direction of B but not yet its strength/magnitude.
2026-10-23.wish: Didn't get through the full lecture notes -- reached B-field direction but not the magnitude/strength calculation in Section 2. Carries over to Monday (Oct 26).
2026-10-23.struggled: Kickoff assumed the B-field-from-a-line-of-charge formula/direction, but students hadn't seen it in the prep video beforehand.
2026-10-23.landed: The RC discharge time-constant misconception discussion was confusing for students but a good teachable moment -- worth keeping. Framing Biot-Savart as 'Coulomb's law plus a v-cross term' landed well as an intro.
2026-10-23.nextYear: (1) The prep video before this class should actually cover the B-field-from-a-line-of-charge formula/direction, not just assume it -- that gap made today's kickoff harder than it needed to be. (2) Reuse Test 3 next year largely as-is -- see 2026-10-21's entry; it was effective and today's review surfaced real, addressable misconceptions (Kirchhoff junction rule, discharge time constant) rather than evidence the test itself was flawed. (3) In the Biot-Savart intro notes (Section 1 warm-up), trim from three E-field points down to just one -- doing all three is good teaching but took too much time; one point is enough to make the separation-vector/unit-vector point before moving into Biot-Savart itself.

2026-10-21.landed: Average score 41.5/50 -- much easier than Test 2, and students seemed noticeably more confident during it.
2026-10-21.nextYear: Multiple likely factors, not yet disentangled: (1) students generally find circuits more intuitive than the vector-heavy electrostatics material Test 2 covered, (2) Seth gave students sample problems to work from beforehand, (3) students were allowed to bring in their own notes. On (3) specifically: Seth wants to reconsider how much material to let students bring in to tests -- it may be discouraging real studying (students copying from notes rather than learning the material), and he's not confident how much genuine learning happened versus how much was just transcription during the test. Revisit this when prepping the spring term in January, not before.
2026-10-21.notes: Grading retrospective here covers difficulty/confidence only, not a breakdown of which specific problems students struggled with.

2026-10-19.covered: RC circuits review (the designated flex/catch-up day), ahead of Test 3 on Wednesday (Oct 21). Went back over the class notes already made: charge on a capacitor at a single instant, using Kirchhoff's loop rule to write the loop equation for a single loop, adding capacitors together in parallel, and the charging equations for current and charge.
2026-10-19.wish: Wanted to get to problem 4 -- a steady-state case where the resistor values actually matter (Seth thinks it's a good problem) -- but ran out of time. Also didn't get to discharging at all, which still needs to be covered.
2026-10-19.nextYear: Discharging didn't get covered in this review day, and it's not clear from this entry alone whether it was covered earlier in the unit either -- check against the Oct 14 RC-circuits lecture log. The test itself (Test 3, Oct 21) includes a discharge problem (Section 4, Part 2), so confirm students actually saw discharging taught somewhere before being tested on it.

2026-10-12.covered: Started by reminding students of their test rewrites (due next Monday), written homework (due tomorrow, Oct 13), and that online homework had been due the previous evening (Oct 11) -- a lot of deadlines to surface at once. Then went over some Kirchhoff loop problems, which went okay. Ended class starting to go over RC circuits, but didn't have enough time to really get into it -- students have RC-circuit homework due tomorrow (Oct 13), so it remains to be seen how that goes.
2026-10-12.wish: Wanted more time on RC circuits/capacitors -- only started that material before class ended, and students have homework on it due tomorrow.
2026-10-12.landed: Kirchhoff loop problems went okay, not a standout.
2026-10-12.nextYear: Seth is second-guessing whether the Kirchhoff loop problems were the best use of today's class time -- leaning toward wanting to shift more time toward RC circuits/capacitors instead, since that's the topic he feels students need more help understanding.

2026-10-07.covered: Power from a resistor, then started Kirchhoff loops. Worked a circuit with one battery and one resistor in series with two resistors in parallel: reduced it to the equivalent circuit, found the current and voltage for every resistor, then introduced P = I*ΔV and solved for the power through everything. Showed that the total power matches in both directions -- the equivalent circuit's power equals the sum of the individual resistors' powers. Then switched to a classic Kirchhoff loop problem (two batteries, three resistors, a couple of loops) and started writing the first loop equations before class ended.
2026-10-07.wish: Didn't get through the full Kirchhoff loop problem -- class ended partway through writing down the first couple of loop equations.
2026-10-07.landed: The power-equivalence demonstration (equivalent-circuit power = sum of the individual resistors' power) landed well. Introducing P = IΔV here felt important/well-placed.
2026-10-07.nextYear: Still unsure whether Kirchhoff's laws should really be positioned as day 1 of this two-day set. This year, series/parallel formulas + Ohm's law + the other basic rules happened naturally on Monday (Oct 5), and Kirchhoff loops + P=IV filled Wednesday (today) -- worth revisiting whether the planned day-1/day-2 split matches how it actually teaches best. Also: some of the Kirchhoff-problem resistor values gave unrealistically large currents (~3 A) -- redo with resistor values that keep currents in a believable range (kΩ-scale resistors, not values that work out to amps).

2026-10-05.covered: Ohm's law + Kirchhoff's laws (series/parallel intro). Worked through the circuits-intro-notes lecture notes -- definitions, the four rules, Ohm's law, then one resistor (ideal vs. real battery), series, and parallel, each with a derivation and a numeric example. Got through pretty much everything on the notes. Seth felt this lecture went better than recent ones.
2026-10-05.struggled: The Prep 14 video (introducing Kirchhoff's laws and circuits in general) was not recorded in time for this class -- that gap likely made the kickoff a little confusing for students going in without it.
2026-10-05.landed: Using the printed lecture notes (rather than teaching off the board with nothing handed out, as happened the last couple of times) -- Seth felt today's lecture went better.
2026-10-05.nextYear: Make sure the Prep 14 video (Kirchhoff's laws / circuits intro) is actually recorded before this class, not just the written prep -- its absence this year likely confused the kickoff.
2026-10-05.notes: Told students Test 2 would be handed back Wednesday (Oct 7) if possible, with a makeup opportunity for what they got wrong. Written HW 5 wasn't posted until today (Oct 5), so its due date got pushed to after the Oct 9 break (now Oct 12) rather than the original Oct 7 -- not Seth's preferred timing, but a consequence of the late posting. It includes extra-credit problems (Section 2, 1 pt each) alongside the required set.

2026-10-02.struggled: Running long was the headline problem -- no students finished on time. Seth suspects two specific contributors, not yet confirmed: (1) the line-of-charge problem being an analytic (symbolic/calculus) setup may have been too hard, and separately students weren't efficient at that type of calculation generally (this was the first problem on the test, so slowness there likely ate into time for the rest). (2) Several students said afterward they didn't understand the Gauss's law problem -- surprising to Seth since they'd done homework problems in that same vein correctly; true as reported, but he doesn't yet have a clear read on why the disconnect happened on the test itself.
2026-10-02.nextYear: The test was too long -- trim it. Look specifically at whether the line-of-charge analytic problem is worth keeping as-is or needs to be simplified/shortened, and whether more in-class time on efficient technique for that calculation type would help before the next test (rather than just cutting the problem).
2026-10-02.notes: Grading + makeup work for students still to come this term; this entry covers the retrospective on the test's length/difficulty only, not grading outcomes.

2026-09-28.covered: Electric potential. Kickoff was quick and clean, only two questions. Introduced V as charge's version of height -- gravitational PE needs mass + a height reference, EPE needs an amount of charge + a potential reference -- then defined the volt. Started with the infinite line/plane of charge (the algebra students hadn't seen this yet, so introduced it live) before the parallel-plate capacitor: E = eta/eps0 between the plates, 0 outside, brief mention of edge fringing. Worked Knight Example 25.6 (proton speed after crossing a 100 V potential difference); the height analogy for predicting the proton would slow down landed well, and the electron-speeds-up point came across clearly. Closed with potential of a single point charge (1/(4 pi eps0) q/r) and Example 25.9 (two point charges, V at point P); added an ad-hoc example of placing a +1 nC charge at P to make the point that V alone isn't PE -- you still need an actual charge there, and even then it's only relative to another reference point.
2026-09-28.wish: Wanted to show V changing in uniform steps across the capacitor gap (high at the + plate, low at the - plate) right after establishing E is uniform there -- planned but didn't get to it, and Seth felt that stretch of the lecture was disjointed as a result (introduced E is constant but never closed the loop on what that means for V). For the Example 25.6 proton problem, wanted to emphasize two things that got skipped: (1) the potential difference doesn't have to run from 0 to 100 V, those were just the two endpoints in this problem: (2) it doesn't have to come from a uniform field at all -- V could go up and down between the two points, only the net difference matters.
2026-09-28.landed: Kickoff -- fast, only two questions, no wasted time. The mass/height <-> charge/potential-reference analogy in the opening. The 'is the proton speeding up or slowing down' height-analogy reasoning for Example 25.6. The electron-speeds-up contrast landed clearly. The point-charge V calculation into 'that's still not PE, you need a charge there, and even then only relative to another point' -- worth keeping and emphasizing more explicitly next time.
2026-09-28.nextYear: Close the E-is-uniform -> V-changes-linearly loop for the capacitor explicitly (don't just show E is constant and move on -- that's what made this stretch feel disjointed). For Example 25.6, explicitly generalize: the potential difference need not be 0-to-100, and need not come from a uniform field -- could go up and down, only Delta V between the two endpoints matters. Emphasize more: knowing V at a point is not the same as having a PE there -- you need to add a charge, AND that PE is still only relative to wherever else you're comparing it to. Handout format: don't print the full electric-potential-notes skeleton packet for a standard lecture like this one -- just print the problem statements for the 1-2 worked examples (here, Knight 25.6 and 25.9) and have students work them at their seats instead of everything running on the board.
2026-09-28.notes: Open pedagogical question Seth wants to track going forward, not specific to this class day: it's not clear the class-prep questions are actually revealing how much students internalized coming into class. Worth thinking about how to design preps that better surface that, rather than assuming prep completion means the concept landed. Materials: did not hand out the electric-potential-notes skeleton packet -- did the whole lecture on the board instead. In hindsight, wanted students working 1-2 problems themselves during a standard lecture; for this class that would have meant printing just the two worked-example problem statements (25.6, 25.9), not the full notes packet.

materials.name: electric-potential-notes.pdf
materials.note: Built for this day but not handed out -- taught from the board instead. See nextYear/notes: next time, print just the 1-2 example problem statements for students to work, not the full skeleton packet.

2026-09-30.covered: Scheduled as a catch-up/flex day ahead of Test 2 (Oct 2); used it as review rather than new content. Went back to the parallel-plate capacitor and introduced the idea of evenly spaced equipotential surfaces inside it. Asked students to compare the force on a charge at different locations inside the capacitor and ran a short think-pair-share on that, using it to identify where the potential was high vs. low. Leaned on the height analogy: emphasized that if you know the beginning and final height (potential), that alone is enough to get the change in speed of an object -- you don't need anything else. Then worked HW problem 25.26 (a proton shot into a capacitor toward a wall, which turns around and comes back) and discussed how the problem changes if it's an electron instead of a proton. Switched to the electric dipole in a field: torque, the right-hand rule, and relating that to the direction of angular acceleration. Also covered dipole potential energy, with emphasis -- via the worked example -- that the angle given in a problem is not necessarily the angle between the dipole moment and the field, so students have to actually draw it out to get that angle right. Closed by revisiting that the lowest-potential-energy orientation is the thing you actually need to find.
2026-09-30.landed: Students picked up the HW 25.26 proton-vs-electron comparison well.
2026-09-30.wish: Wanted to get to superposition between a point charge's field and a plane/line of charge, but didn't reach it.
2026-09-30.nextYear: Unit-level note, not specific to this review day: across the whole electrostatics unit this year, almost no class time went to conductors & insulators or to polarization problems. The idea was introduced briefly in lecture but never followed up with a single class question on it. Make sure conductors/insulators and polarization get real class time and actual questions next year, not just a passing mention.

2026-09-25.covered: Kickoff + HW feedback, then welcomed the two sections back together after 3 lectures split. Stressed that F, E, U, and V are all linear quantities that obey superposition - e.g. the E field from a line of charge plus a point charge is just the vector sum of their individual contributions - and that this will be on Test 2. Then EPE: compared gravity and electrostatics side by side. Ball with U=mgh, then U in a hole of depth d (the -mgd sign flip is genuinely counterintuitive to them, good discussion). Constant E field with + and - charges. Full Newtonian gravitation - they hadn't seen the PE form before, only the near-Earth value - graphed PE for Earth and Moon and discussed why it's negative, compared back to electrostatics. Finished with U = -p . E for a dipole in a constant field.
2026-09-25.wish: Wanted more time for the dipole discussion (U = -p . E) - it was landing really well right when time ran out.
2026-09-25.landed: The gravity-hole / electrostatics side-by-side comparison worked well, especially the sign-flip discussion. Universal gravitation PE graph (Earth-Moon) plus the 'why is it negative' discussion also landed.
2026-09-25.notes: Did NOT hand out the fill-in-the-blank electric-pe-notes skeleton handout - decided in the moment it might read as too much like a 'high school class' for this material. Worked the derivations from the mocked-up notes on the whiteboard instead, without the printed scaffold. Kickoff itself was better-scoped than the last one and wrapped in just a couple minutes.

2026-09-09.covered: Test 1, in class. Four problems: standing waves in a pipe (15 pts, five multiple-choice parts), an oscillating spring (20 pts), a traveling wave (15 pts), and a 5-point extra-credit two-speaker interference problem. 50 points plus 5 extra credit.
2026-09-09.struggled: The oscillating spring gave people the most trouble by far. It was also the heaviest problem at 20 points, and the one that asked them to go from initial conditions (x0 and v0) all the way to an explicit x(t) = A cos(wt + phi), including the phase constant, and then sketch it.
2026-09-09.nextYear: Three things. (1) The oscillating-spring problem is where the points were lost - give the x0/v0 to amplitude-and-phase-constant chain more class time before the test, since it is the one place students have to carry a multi-step result forward rather than plug into a single formula. (2) Timing was close to right but not comfortable: consider trimming a part, most likely one of the five standing-wave multiple-choice items. (3) HOMEWORK STRUCTURE: this test date is the slot where Written HW 2 would naturally have been due, so it got pushed to Sep 16 and the pre-test week carried no written HW. In previous years there was an extra written HW before the test covering that material. This year the HW1-practice worksheet was built to fill the gap. Next year, fold the HW1-practice problems into Written HW 1 so the material is assessed before the test rather than patched in with a worksheet.
2026-09-09.notes: Pacing: most students finished with time to spare, but some were still working when time was called. Per-segment minutes are not meaningful for a test day.

2026-09-21.covered: Opened with a brief lecture on flux, which carried straight into finishing the kickoff as a class. Then a long stretch lecturing on the torque on an electric dipole: defining the dipole moment and deriving tau = p x E. Closed by giving students a little time to start the written HW.
2026-09-21.cut: Time for students to start the written HW in class got squeezed by the dipole lecture.
2026-09-21.wish: More class time for them to get going on the written HW.
2026-09-21.nextYear: The dipole-torque derivation (dipole moment, tau = p x E) took a good deal of time on its own - budget for it explicitly rather than folding it in behind flux. None of it involved any calculus, so it does not need to be split by track: run the dipole material with the full class (230 and 235 together) and save the split for the day's calculus-dependent content. The electric-dipole-in-field sim is now linked from this day; use it.
2026-09-21.notes: Did not use the electric dipole sim. It turned out one already existed and had since Sep 15 - electric-dipole-in-field, covering tau = p x E, U = -p.E and the rotational-pendulum swing - but it had never been added to the catalog, so it was effectively invisible. Fixed the same evening: added to the catalog, and wired to Sep 21 in the course map and schedule alongside the flux sim. Oct 30's dipole entry was a slug-less placeholder and now points at dipole-field-and-torque. Minutes per segment were not recorded for this day.

2026-09-23.covered: The kickoff made clear students had not internalized Gauss's law, so pivoted to the skeleton worksheet (gauss-applications-notes.tex) and worked through the end of its first section before going back and answering the kickoff questions. That took longer than planned; only reached the point-charge example by the end of class. Derived E for a point charge from Gauss's law and emphasized it holds for any spherically symmetric charge distribution - even a non-uniform one - as long as the distribution respects the symmetry.
2026-09-23.cut: Did not get to the shell, or any of the other symmetry examples (line, sheet, sphere) in the worksheet.
2026-09-23.struggled: Came into class not having internalized Gauss's law itself, which is what forced the pivot back to re-teaching it before the kickoff could be answered.
2026-09-23.nextYear: Make sure students understand Gauss's law itself before this lecture (e.g. via the kickoff or a prior activity) so class time can go to the worked symmetry examples instead of re-teaching the law first. Also, KO 11 (Fields from Gauss's Law) itself was too long/hard - it likely contributed to the pivot described above. Shorten it or make it easier next year.

No .tex source in the repo - the PDF is the copy handed back in this conversation. Test rules allowed five pages of students' own newly made notes and a graphing calculator, nothing else, so the equation sheet below was a study resource, not a test aid.

materials.name: Equation sheet: Oscillations & Waves

demosWishlist.name: Ukulele
demosWishlist.note: Per Seth 2026-10-01: would be good to have for next year's waves-unit demos (plucked string -> standing wave) -- this year's waves demos were limited to standing waves in a pipe.

demosWishlist.name: Oersted's experiment (compass deflects near a current-carrying wire)
demosWishlist.note: Suggested 2026-10-16 for Oct 23 (Magnetic fields + Biot-Savart), the first magnetism class day. Flip the current direction and watch the compass deflection reverse. Cheap, fast, historically the original discovery of this whole unit.

demosWishlist.name: Iron filings around a straight current-carrying wire
demosWishlist.note: Suggested 2026-10-16 for Oct 23 (Magnetic fields + Biot-Savart), paired with Oersted's experiment same day. Filings on a card with the wire through a hole, tap to reveal concentric circles.

demosWishlist.name: Iron filings around a loop / solenoid
demosWishlist.note: Suggested 2026-10-16 for Oct 26 (B from a line + a loop). Contrast the single-wire circles with a loop's dipole-like pattern and a solenoid's uniform interior -- same filings technique as the Oct 23 demo, different source geometry.

demosWishlist.name: Solenoid field-uniformity probe (compass or Hall probe along the axis, then outside)
demosWishlist.note: Suggested 2026-10-16 for Oct 28 (Ampere's law). Constant reading inside, near-zero just outside -- makes the symmetry argument Ampere's law leans on tangible. A toroid, if the department has one, is an even more dramatic version (field essentially zero everywhere outside the torus).

demosWishlist.name: Simple DC motor (wire loop on an axle between magnet poles + battery)
demosWishlist.note: Suggested 2026-10-16 for Oct 30 (Magnetic dipoles + torque). The classic torque-on-a-current-loop demo; a split-ring commutator keeps it spinning continuously instead of just twitching toward alignment. Doubles as material for the Nov 6 applications day if not fully used here.

demosWishlist.name: CRT or e/m tube beam deflection by a magnet
demosWishlist.note: Suggested 2026-10-16 for Nov 2 (Magnetic force on charges). Bringing a magnet near a CRT bends the beam -- direct, visual F = qv x B. An e/m tube (if available) is better still since the beam curves into a full circle, tying straight into r = mv/(qB). Needs department inventory check -- not confirmed available.

demosWishlist.name: Jumping-wire demo (current-carrying wire between horseshoe-magnet poles)
demosWishlist.note: Suggested 2026-10-16 for Nov 4 (Magnetic force + torque on wires). Wire visibly jumps when current flows (F = IL x B); reversing current reverses the jump direction. A two-parallel-wires attract/repel demo is a good second option the same day, and ties into how the Ampere itself is historically defined.

demosWishlist.name: Cut-open speaker or galvanometer
demosWishlist.note: Suggested 2026-10-16 for Nov 6 (Magnetism in action -- applications). A real voice coil or D'Arsonval movement makes the force-on-a-current-carrying-wire-in-a-field idea concrete as an actual device; pairs well with revisiting the DC motor from Oct 30.
